estimates.title: Age-specific transmission dynamics under suppression control measures during SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.2 epidemic
estimates.notes: Estimated using an age-structured SEIR model with social contact patterns and the next-generation matrix. estimates.title: Estimation of the incubation period of COVID-19 using viral load data
estimates.notes: Original research using longitudinal viral load data from 30 hospitalized patients and a viral dynamics model to hindcast the time of infection. Estimated a median incubation period of 5.85 days (95% CI 5.05–6.77).

estimates.title: Inferred duration of infectious period of SARS-CoV-2: rapid scoping review and analysis of available evidence for asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19 cases

estimates.title: Inferred duration of infectious period of SARS-CoV-2: rapid scoping review and analysis of available evidence for asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19 cases

estimates.title: Inferred duration of infectious period of SARS-CoV-2: rapid scoping review and analysis of available evidence for asymptomatic and symptomatic COVID-19 cases
estimates.notes: Mean 13.4 days (95% CI 10.9–15.8) from symptom onset to first of two negative RT-PCR tests, pooled across 15 virological studies (high heterogeneity I²>75%). RT-PCR positivity outlasts true infectious potential by approximately 2–6 days; viral culture studies indicate most transmission ceases by day 8–10 post-symptom onset.

estimates.population: Mild-to-moderate symptomatic cases — viral culture / true infectiousness
estimates.title: The duration of infectiousness of individuals infected with SARS-CoV-2
estimates.notes: Rapid review integrating viral culture, contact tracing, and viral shedding data. Concluded that mild-to-moderate COVID-19 patients are highly unlikely to remain infectious beyond 10 days post-symptom onset; most transmission occurs earlier. Viral culture success (the gold-standard infectiousness proxy) drops sharply after day 8. Note: this is a lower estimate than the Byrne et al. RT-PCR-based figure above because culture positivity declines faster than PCR positivity.

consensus.notes: Using global estimate of IFR.

estimates.title: Case fatality rate of COVID-19: a systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Aimed to assess the pooled CFR of COVID-19.

estimates.title: Infection fatality rate of COVID-19 inferred from seroprevalence data
estimates.notes: Systematic review/evidence synthesis of seroprevalence studies and national estimates available through 9 September 2020. Included 61 studies (74 estimates) plus 8 preliminary national estimates. Across 51 locations, the median inferred COVID-19 infection fatality rate (IFR) was 0.27%, with a corrected median of 0.23%. Reported IFRs ranged from 0.00% to 1.63% (corrected range 0.00% to 1.54%). Reflects largely ancestral / early-pandemic SARS-CoV-2 before later variants became dominant.

estimates.population: All ages, China, age-stratified (0% in <10y to 14.8% in 80+y)
estimates.title: Global Covid-19 Case Fatality Rates
estimates.notes: Overall CFR 2.3% (1023 deaths / 44,672 confirmed cases). No deaths in age <10y. CFR 14.8% in 80+y. CFR 0.9% in those with no comorbidities vs 49% case fatality in critical cases. Age-stratified CFRs: 10–19y 0.18%, 20–49y 0.32%, 50–59y 1.3%, 60–69y 3.6%, 70–79y 8.0%, 80+y 14.8%.

estimates.title: Global Covid-19 Case Fatality Rates
estimates.notes: Verity et al. estimated IFR 0.66% (95% CI 0.39–1.33%) using age-stratified CFR from China plus 1,334 individual cases identified outside mainland China. Imperial College London adjusted this to 0.9% (95% CrI 0.4–1.4%) for the UK, accounting for non-uniform attack rate.

estimates.population: All ages, Iceland — highest per-capita testing rate globally at time of report
estimates.title: Global Covid-19 Case Fatality Rates
estimates.notes: 10 deaths in 1,798 confirmed cases (CFR 0.56%). Assuming 1% of population (364,000) infected gives IFR ~0.3%. Authors note Iceland's test-and-quarantine measures may have shielded elderly, and lag between infection and death means estimates may shift. Considered the most reliable early IFR estimate due to Iceland's near-complete population testing.

estimates.title: Estimating the infection fatality rate of emerging diseases using a regression approach applied to global COVID-19 cases
estimates.notes: Regression-based estimate of the global infection fatality rate (IFR) for early COVID-19 using case fatality rates and population testing data across 139 countries affected before May 2020. Estimated a conservative global IFR of 0.90% (95% CI 0.70–1.16%). Reflects largely ancestral / early-pandemic SARS-CoV-2.

estimates.population: General population under initial COVID-19 mitigation / lockdown measures

estimates.country: Multiple countries (primarily Europe, with some non-European settings)
estimates.notes: Systematic review of 12 studies reporting social contact patterns during the COVID-19 pandemic. During the initial mitigation period in spring 2020, most study settings reported mean contact rates between 2 and 5 contacts per person per day, compared with pre-COVID rates of 7 to 26 contacts per person per day. Reflects contact behavior under lockdown / suppression measures rather than intrinsic baseline contact rates.

estimates.population: General population before COVID-19 / pre-pandemic baseline
estimates.title: Rapid Review of Social Contact Patterns During the COVID-19 Pandemic
estimates.notes: The review summarized pre-COVID comparison data from the included studies and reported pre-pandemic contact rates ranging from 7 to 26 contacts per person per day. This is useful as a baseline comparator for contact behavior before distancing measures.

estimates.title: Nationally Representative Social Contact Patterns among U.S. adults, August 2020-April 2021
estimates.notes: National probability survey of U.S. adults with self-reported daily contacts. Mean daily contacts were 13.9 (baseline, Aug–Dec 2020) and 14.5 (follow-up, Mar–Apr 2021). This reflects contact behavior after the earliest lockdown period and under evolving mitigation measures, not pre-pandemic baseline contact rates.

estimates.population: General population in Chinese provinces outside Hubei after lockdown lifting

estimates.notes: Contact survey conducted in March 2020 after lockdowns were lifted in Chinese provinces outside Hubei. Participants reported 2.3 contacts per day (IQR 1.0–3.0), suggesting that contact behavior remained strongly reduced even after formal lockdown ended.

consensus.notes: Represents approximate duration of substantial protection against reinfection after prior SARS-CoV-2 infection in the pre-Omicron / early-pandemic period. This is not the same as duration of detectable antibodies or T-cell memory, and protection is shorter against immune-evasive variants such as Omicron.

estimates.title: Quantifying the risk of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection over time
estimates.notes: Systematic review of 11 large cohort studies of SARS-CoV-2 reinfection. Reinfection remained uncommon, and no clear evidence of waning was observed over follow-up periods extending to more than 10 months in several studies. Useful as an estimate of at least ~10 months of protection against reinfection during the early pandemic.

estimates.title: The prevalence of adaptive immunity to COVID-19 and reinfection after recovery – a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 54 studies from 18 countries. Around 90% of recovered individuals retained evidence of immunological memory at 6–8 months after recovery, and reinfection prevalence remained low. Good source for a conservative lower-bound estimate of post-infection immune duration.

estimates.title: SARS-CoV-2 reinfections: Overview of efficacy and duration of natural and hybrid immunity
estimates.notes: Narrative review summarizing evidence that natural immunity after SARS-CoV-2 infection provides strong protection against reinfection for at least one year, with only moderate waning before Omicron. Protection against severe disease appears to last longer than protection against infection.

estimates.title: Durability of Vaccine-Induced and Natural Immunity Against COVID-19: A Narrative Review
estimates.notes: Narrative review summarizing studies of waning protection after infection and vaccination. Reports high protection from prior infection over at least 7 months in meta-analyses and several studies showing little significant waning through roughly 8–12 months in pre-Omicron settings.

consensus.notes: Represents the proportion of SARS-CoV-2 infections that remain asymptomatic throughout the full course of infection. Estimates vary substantially depending on follow-up, age structure, testing strategy, and whether presymptomatic cases were excluded. For ancestral / early-pandemic SARS-CoV-2, a reasonable overall consensus is ~35%, with lower estimates (~20%) from stricter early reviews and higher estimates (~44%) from later age-inclusive meta-analyses.

estimates.title: Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection: A systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of more than 350 studies. Estimated that 35.1% of SARS-CoV-2 infections never developed clinical symptoms and were therefore truly asymptomatic. Distinguished asymptomatic infections from presymptomatic infections and removed index cases to reduce bias.

estimates.title: Occurrence and transmission potential of asymptomatic and presymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infections: A living systematic review and meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Living systematic review and meta-analysis of 79 studies. Estimated that 20% of SARS-CoV-2 infections remained asymptomatic throughout infection. Prediction interval was wide because of substantial heterogeneity and risk of selection bias across studies.

estimates.title: Asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 Infection by Age: A Global Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
estimates.notes: Global systematic review and meta-analysis of studies conducted during 2020 before routine vaccination. Across 14,850 infected individuals, 44.1% remained asymptomatic throughout infection. Also found strong age variation, with asymptomatic infection more common in children and younger adults than in the elderly.

consensus.notes: Consensus reflects heterogeneous literature on mumps transmissibility. Most commonly cited general-population estimates fall around 4–12, including review and modeling studies from the UK, Europe, South Korea, and the United States. A higher estimate of 19.3 was reported from a Bayesian age-structured pre-vaccination UK serologic modeling study and is retained as an upper-bound historical estimate rather than a typical modern value. A representative typical R0 of 10 is used here to reflect the central tendency of commonly cited historical/general-population estimates while acknowledging substantial model- and setting-dependent variation.

Most transmission likely occurs before and within 5 days of parotitis onset, supporting a conventional infectious period centered on the interval around symptom onset.

consensus.notes: Published estimates of the basic reproduction number (R₀) for varicella generally range from approximately 5.5 to 10. Primary modeling studies have estimated R₀ around 5.7 in South Korea, while reviews and public health literature commonly cite values of 8–10. A typical value of 8 is consistent with the broader epidemiologic literature and is commonly used for herd immunity calculations.

estimates.title: Effect of Routine Varicella Immunization on the Epidemiology and Immunogenicity of Varicella and Shingles
estimates.notes: The basic reproduction number of varicella is thought to range from 8 to 10, indicating that the current immunization coverage in Japan is insufficient to prevent varicella, and that additional efforts are needed to promote vaccination against varicella.

estimates.title: Estimating the basic reproductive number of varicella in South Korea incorporating social contact patterns and seroprevalence

Published estimates of the basic reproduction number (R₀) for pertussis span approximately 5.3–17. Lower values (5.3–11.5) are derived from modern transmission models incorporating serological data, vaccination, and social contact patterns, whereas public health agencies and expert reviews consistently cite 12–17 (commonly 15–17) as the historical R₀ in a fully susceptible population. For epidemiological modeling of an immunologically naïve population, values around 14–15 are most commonly used.

The study concluded that infections in individuals with waning immunity drive most transmission to children.

estimates.title: How Flu Spreads
estimates.notes: CDC states symptoms typically begin about two days (range 1-4 days) after influenza virus infects a person's respiratory tract. Also notes people can be contagious starting ~1 day before symptom onset, and remain contagious through 5-7 days after becoming sick, with the first 3 days being most contagious.

estimates.title: Contagious Period for Influenza (Flu)

consensus.notes: Symptomatic case-fatality rate for seasonal influenza is low and varies substantially by season severity and age group. Mortality is heavily concentrated in adults 65+ (about two-thirds of deaths in recent U.S. seasons) and is far lower in children and young adults. The typical value (0.07%) reflects symptomatic-case denominators for seasonal influenza. Case definition drives fatality rate estimates by orders of magnitude: a systematic review of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic found estimates ranging from ~0.001-0.01% using an infections denominator, ~0-1.2% using a symptomatic-cases denominator, and ~0-13.5% using a laboratory-confirmed-cases denominator, with the latter most prone to ascertainment bias since testing is typically reserved for more severe presentations. Any fatality rate figure should be interpreted alongside its denominator definition.

estimates.title: 2023-2024 Influenza Season Summary: Severity Assessment, Burden and Burden Prevented
estimates.notes: CDC estimated 40 million symptomatic illnesses and 28,000 deaths for the 2023-2024 season (~0.07% symptomatic CFR). Adults 65+ accounted for only 8% of medical visits but 68% of deaths.

estimates.title: Case fatality risk of influenza A(H1N1pdm09): a systematic review
estimates.notes: Wong, Kelly, Ip, Wu, Leung & Cowling, Epidemiology. Systematic review of 77 estimates from 50 studies on the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. When the denominator was total infections (including asymptomatic/subclinical), point estimates ranged from 1-10 deaths per 100,000 infections (0.001%-0.01%) — comparable in magnitude to seasonal influenza IFR estimates.

estimates.title: Case fatality risk of influenza A(H1N1pdm09): a systematic review
estimates.notes: When the denominator was symptomatic cases, point estimates ranged from 0-1,200 deaths per 100,000 symptomatic cases (0%-1.2%). Risk based on symptomatic cases increased substantially with age. This is roughly an order of magnitude higher than infection-based estimates and reflects the exclusion of asymptomatic/mild infections from the denominator.

estimates.title: Case fatality risk of influenza A(H1N1pdm09): a systematic review
estimates.notes: When the denominator was laboratory-confirmed cases only, point estimates ranged from 0-13,500 deaths per 100,000 confirmed cases (0%-13.5%) — the highest and most heterogeneous set of estimates, since testing was typically reserved for more severe presentations, inflating apparent severity. Authors caution this reflects a strong ascertainment bias rather than true disease severity.

Homologous strain protection wanes gradually over several years, but influenza's rapid antigenic drift means functional protection against currently circulating strains erodes much faster in practice (often within a single year or two), since new variants can partially evade prior immunity.

estimates.title: Review Article: The Fraction of Influenza Virus Infections That Are Asymptomatic: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

estimates.title: The Spectrum of Influenza in Children
